title: Why Rules Are More Important Than Consequences
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin argues that teachers who chase ever more creative or punitive consequences are solving the wrong problem, since there is no magic set of consequences — what actually matters is well-taught, consistently enforced rules. He explains that clearly defined rules let students experience misbehavior as a choice they made, which produces genuine responsibility and remorse rather than resentment toward the teacher. He identifies two disciplines that make this work: teaching rules so thoroughly that no gray area exists about what breaks them, and enforcing them with total consistency so students trust that a consequence will always follow. Together, he argues, these two commitments free students to focus on learning because they know accountability is fair, predictable, and entirely of their own making — a mechanism he calls 'the real magic' of classroom management.
points: There is no magic set of consequences; effectiveness comes from the rules themselves, not their severity or creativity.
Clearly taught rules let students experience misbehavior as their own choice, producing genuine responsibility.
Teach rules so thoroughly that there is no gray area about what does and doesn't count as breaking them.
Enforce rules with total consistency — every time, not most of the time — or they carry little meaning.
When both conditions are met, students are freed to trust the teacher's leadership and focus on learning.
quotes: Because there are no magic consequences. They don’t exist. There are best practices—which we’ve developed here at SCM—but virtually any configuration of consequences can work.
Taught in a certain way, rules make every act of misbehavior a choice students know full well they’re making.
Because when students view misbehavior as a choice, they take responsibility for it. They feel genuine remorse. They reflect on their mistakes and privately vow not to make them again.
You must consistently enforce your rules or they mean very little. Consistent doesn’t mean most of the time. It means all the time.
With both sticklers in play, your students will know that misbehavior is 100% their choice and own doing.
This is the real magic and secret to exceptional classroom management .
